subject: Neurology
vignette: A physiology instructor is demonstrating how to isolate individual extraocular muscles. She wants to test the right superior oblique muscle specifically, using the principle that the obliques are tested with the eye turned in the direction opposite their name.
question: In which direction of gaze should the patient look to best isolate the right superior oblique?

options.text: Up and to the left with the eye elevated

explanation_correct: The obliques are tested with gaze opposite to their name: the right superior oblique is best isolated when the patient looks to the left (the opposite side) and downward, the direction in which the superior oblique acts. This follows the rule LR6SO4R3, with the superior oblique supplied by CN IV. Looking down and to the left places the right eye in the position that maximally challenges superior oblique function.

explanation_incorrect.A: Looking up and to the right tests muscles whose action is elevation and abduction, not the depressing, intorting superior oblique.
explanation_incorrect.B: Looking down and to the right tests the right inferior rectus rather than the superior oblique, which acts with gaze to the opposite side.
explanation_incorrect.C: Elevated gaze would engage the inferior oblique, an elevator, rather than the superior oblique, which depresses the eye.
explanation_incorrect.D: Straight-up gaze does not isolate a single oblique and would mainly test the elevators supplied by CN III.

educationalObjective: The obliques are tested with opposite gaze; the right superior oblique is isolated by looking down and to the left.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A first-year resident is reviewing the mnemonic LR6SO4R3 before an eye examination. She wants to confirm which extraocular muscle is correctly paired with its innervating cranial nerve.
question: Which of the following muscle-and-nerve pairings is correct?
explanation_correct: The mnemonic LR6SO4R3 states that the lateral rectus is innervated by CN VI, the superior oblique by CN IV, and all remaining extraocular muscles by CN III. Thus lateral rectus paired with CN VI is correct. The obliques are tested with gaze opposite their name, and the inferior oblique is tested looking up.

explanation_incorrect.A: The superior oblique is supplied by CN IV, not CN III; only the 'rest' of the muscles are CN III.
explanation_incorrect.C: The inferior oblique is one of the muscles supplied by CN III, not CN IV.
explanation_incorrect.D: The medial rectus is innervated by CN III; CN VI supplies only the lateral rectus.
explanation_incorrect.E: The superior rectus is supplied by CN III, while CN IV supplies the superior oblique.

educationalObjective: LR6SO4R3: CN VI innervates lateral rectus, CN IV innervates superior oblique, and CN III innervates the rest.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A 22-year-old man is struck in the right eye by a baseball and cannot look upward with that eye. He also reports numbness over the right cheek. CT shows a fracture of the orbital floor with soft tissue herniation.
question: Which extraocular muscle is most likely entrapped in this injury?
explanation_correct: A blowout fracture of the orbital floor commonly entraps the inferior rectus muscle and orbital fat, limiting upward gaze in the affected eye. The fracture can also injure the infraorbital nerve, which explains the cheek numbness. The orbital floor lies directly beneath the inferior rectus, making it the muscle at risk.

explanation_incorrect.A: The superior rectus lies along the orbital roof, not the floor, and would not be entrapped by a floor fracture.
explanation_incorrect.B: The lateral rectus runs along the lateral orbital wall and is not adjacent to the orbital floor.
explanation_incorrect.D: The superior oblique is located superiorly near the trochlea and is not in contact with the orbital floor.
explanation_incorrect.E: The medial rectus lies on the medial wall and is not the muscle typically trapped in a blowout fracture of the floor.

educationalObjective: Orbital floor (blowout) fractures trap the inferior rectus and can injure the infraorbital nerve, causing impaired upward gaze and cheek numbness.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A 4-year-old girl has a constant inward deviation of the right eye. Her pediatrician warns that if it is not corrected, she may develop reduced vision in that eye from disuse. The family asks which type of strabismus she has and what complication is meant by 'lazy eye.'
question: Which of the following best describes the most common type of strabismus in children and its principal complication?

options.text: Esotropia; amblyopia from maldevelopment of the visual cortex
Exophoria; diplopia from lateral rectus palsy
Esophoria; anopia from optic nerve transection

explanation_correct: Esotropia, an inward deviation of the eye toward the nose, is the most common type of strabismus in children. Persistent misalignment can cause amblyopia, or 'lazy eye,' in which decreased visual acuity results from maldevelopment of the visual cortex due to abnormal visual experience early in life. It is typically unilateral and underscores the need for early correction.

explanation_incorrect.B: Exotropia is an outward deviation and is not the most common childhood strabismus; nystagmus is not the definition of lazy eye.
explanation_incorrect.C: Hypertropia is a vertical deviation and does not produce the ptosis of sympathetic denervation seen in Horner syndrome.
explanation_incorrect.D: Exophoria is a latent outward deviation; diplopia from a lateral rectus palsy reflects CN VI dysfunction, not amblyopia.
explanation_incorrect.E: Esophoria is a latent inward deviation, while anopia from optic nerve transection is complete monocular blindness, not cortical maldevelopment.

educationalObjective: Esotropia is the most common childhood strabismus and can cause unilateral amblyopia from abnormal early visual experience.
